questions.prompt: Metchnikoff combined two big ideas to predict that an immune system must exist. Which two?

options.text: Koch's postulates and Gram's differential stain
Pasteurization and Jenner's smallpox vaccination
Germ theory (Pasteur/Koch) and evolution (Darwin)
Spontaneous generation and germ theory (Pasteur)

questions.explanation: If microbes evolve to cause disease, hosts must evolve defenses.

questions.prompt: Why did scientists first doubt Metchnikoff's phagocytes were host cells?

options.text: They only appeared in starfish larvae that were already dead
They looked and behaved like free-crawling parasitic amoebas
They were far too small to see with microscopes of the time
They contained chlorophyll, so they had to be algae instead

questions.explanation: White blood cells are among the only body cells that live untethered.

questions.prompt: A patient on antibiotics develops a vaginal yeast infection. Which first-line defense was disrupted?

options.text: The lacrimal apparatus that flushes and drains the eyes
Sebum production by the sebaceous glands of the skin
Resident microbiota (L. acidophilus) and the acid it makes
The ciliary escalator that clears mucus from the airway

questions.explanation: Without Lactobacillus's lactic acid, pH rises and Candida grows.

questions.prompt: A burn patient loses large areas of skin. Which protective features are lost along with it?

options.text: Circulating neutrophils and tissue macrophages in the blood
Dryness, salt, acidic sebum, shedding, and S. epidermidis
Gastric acid in the stomach and lysozyme in the tears
Mucus, beating cilia, and goblet cells along the trachea

questions.explanation: Intact skin is the best barrier, and burns make it a portal of entry.

questions.prompt: Which statement about antimicrobial fluids is FALSE?

options.text: Urine is the most acidic body fluid, at about pH 2.
Sebum lowers skin pH to about 3–5.
Sweat leaves salt behind when it dries.
Earwax is acidic because it contains sebum.
Saliva contains IgA antibodies as well as lysozyme.

questions.explanation: Gastric juice is pH ~2; urine is about 6.

questions.prompt: Why does dry, cracked skin increase infection risk even without a cut?

options.text: Dry skin has a neutral pH that lets most bacteria grow
Dry skin is colonized by far more S. aureus than S. epidermidis
Dry skin produces much less lysozyme in its sweat
Cracks become portals of entry; sebum keeps skin pliable

questions.explanation: Sebum lubricates skin so it doesn't break open.

questions.prompt: Where does material wiped from the eye by blinking end up?

options.text: Into the bloodstream, where neutrophils engulf any microbes
Through the nasolacrimal duct into the nose, then often swallowed
Into the ear canal, where acidic earwax traps and destroys it
Into the sebaceous glands of the eyelids, where sebum digests it

questions.prompt: Which change happens because histamine is a vasodilator?

options.text: Blood pressure drops
White blood cells stay in the blood
Blood pressure rises
Vessels become watertight

questions.explanation: Wider vessels lower peripheral resistance; that's why falling BP can signal infection.

questions.prompt: Why do macrophages outlast neutrophils at an infection site?

options.text: They arrive only after the infection is over, so they never fill up
They don't actually eat bacteria; they only release histamine
They digest bacteria and exocytose the waste instead of bursting
They are protected from bursting by a thick carbohydrate capsule

questions.prompt: Phagocytosis by a macrophage is considered NONspecific even though it uses receptors. Why?

options.text: Toll-like receptors recognize molecules shared by many microbes
Macrophages only ever eat one species of bacterium each
Toll-like receptors are only used by T cells, not by macrophages
Macrophages make their own antibodies to any antigen they meet

questions.explanation: Recognizing a common sugar isn't recognizing a specific antigen.

questions.prompt: Which pathogen feature from Module 19 directly blocks the first step of phagocytosis?

options.text: A slippery capsule that keeps phagocytes from grabbing it
Siderophores that steal iron from the host's red blood cells
Collagenase that digests connective tissue around the site
Hemolysins that lyse red blood cells in the infected tissue

questions.prompt: Why does the body clot blood around an infection site?

options.text: To lower the local temperature and slow bacteria
To produce histamine that starts inflammation
To feed the bacteria so neutrophils can find them
To wall in and contain the infection (an abscess)

questions.explanation: Clotting contains; a scab later protects the healing site.

questions.prompt: Which outcome is most likely after a large boil heals?

options.text: No trace at all, just like a small pimple that heals
A permanent abscess full of pus that never drains
Loss of all normal flora on that area of the skin
A scar, because lots of damaged tissue must be filled in

questions.explanation: Small pimples heal without a trace; large areas fill with scar tissue.

questions.prompt: Explain how sweat protects the skin in two ways.
questions.explanation: It contains lysozyme, which digests peptidoglycan, and when it evaporates it leaves salt behind, making skin too salty for most bacteria.

questions.prompt: List the steps of phagocytosis by a macrophage, naming the structure formed at each stage.
questions.explanation: Toll-like receptors bind the microbe (e.g., mannose/LPS) → pseudopods surround it → phagosome forms → lysosome fuses → phagolysosome digests it with hydrolytic enzymes → waste released by exocytosis.
